# What R is {#sec-overview .unnumbered}

R is a language for statistics and data analysis, with dynamic types, in which
the vector is the basic value and the data frame the central structure. Models
are written as formulas, such as `y ~ x`, and the base installation already
brings the statistical methods, the tables, and the plots that a data analysis
needs. Beyond it there are more than twenty thousand packages: CRAN, a curated
archive whose packages must pass automatic checks on every release, and
Bioconductor, the packages for genomics and other high-throughput biology.

R is the language of statisticians and of whole fields, such as bioinformatics,
ecology, and epidemiology, for analyses, publication graphics (ggplot2),
reports (Quarto, R Markdown), small web applications (Shiny), and packages that
carry a new statistical method to its users. It is weaker as a general-purpose
language: the base language has grown inconsistencies, and services, command
line tools, and long-running programs are mostly written in other languages.
Much of the work goes to compiled code, and R code that loops over single
elements is slow like Python code that does, so write whole-vector expressions
(@sec-vectors).

Working in R comes down to a mental model (@sec-model), a small set of syntax
(@sec-syntax), and a few tools (@sec-tooling). The rules at the end (@sec-rules)
apply the principles to R. The comparison with [](python.qmd) is noted where the
two differ, because many readers know both.

Checked against R 4.3, renv 1.2, testthat 3.2, and roxygen2 7.3.

rule.

::: {.glance}
| No. | Rule | In one line |

| [-@sec-seq] | [](#sec-seq) | Loop with `seq_len()` and `seq_along()`, not with `1:n`. |
| [-@sec-na-rm] | [](#sec-na-rm) | Decide what happens to `NA` explicitly, and never set `na.rm = TRUE` by reflex. |

:::


# How R thinks {#sec-model}

Four facts explain most of the surprises of R in research software: everything
is a vector (@sec-vectors), values are copied and not shared (@sec-copy),
missing values are values (@sec-na), and a package is either attached or
called by name (@sec-attach).


## Everything is a vector {#sec-vectors}

R has no scalars: `5` is a vector of length one, and operations work on whole
vectors, which makes a loop over single elements unnecessary. Indexing starts
at 1, a range includes both ends, and a negative index drops elements:

```r
values <- c(2.5, 3.1, 4.0)   # a vector: the basic value
values[1]                    # 2.5, the first element
values[-1]                   # 3.1 4.0, all but the first
values[values > 3]           # 3.1 4.0, by a condition
values * 2 + 1               # 6.0 7.2 9.0, element by element
```

Three behaviors give a plausible, wrong result instead of an error. An index
beyond the end gives `NA`, not an error: `values[10]` is `NA`. A shorter vector
is recycled to the length of a longer one, with a warning only when the longer
length is not a multiple of the shorter: `1:6 + 1:2` silently gives
`2 4 4 6 6 8`. And `1:n` counts down when `n` is 0, as `1:0` is `c(1, 0)`
(@sec-seq).


## Values are copied, not shared {#sec-copy}

R copies a value when it is changed, and shares it until then. After
`b <- a`, a change to `b` leaves `a` as it was, and a function that changes its
argument changes only its own copy:

```r
a <- c(1, 2, 3)
b <- a
b[1] <- 0
a                  # 1 2 3, unchanged

f <- function(v) { v[1] <- 99; v }
f(a)               # 99 2 3
a                  # 1 2 3, unchanged
```

That makes R safe against the defect of
[](../principles/design.qmd#sec-mutation) by default, the opposite of
[](python.qmd). The exceptions are the objects that are changed in place:
environments, R6 and reference classes, and the `:=` operator of data.table.
Treat their functions as mutating, and document it.


## NA is a value {#sec-na}

`NA` is the missing value in vectors of every type, and it is infectious: an
operation on an `NA` gives `NA`, so `sum(c(1, NA))` is `NA`, and so is
`NA == NA`. Test with `is.na()`. `NaN` (not a number) and `NULL` (no object,
not a missing value) are different things.

Most summary functions give `NA` for a vector with an `NA` unless called with
`na.rm = TRUE`, which drops them. The first is loud, the second silent, so
dropping must be a decision (@sec-na-rm). A second trap is indexing with a
condition that has `NA`:

```r
df <- data.frame(station = c("A", "A", "B"), temp_c = c(20.1, 22.3, NA))
df[df$temp_c > 21, ]            # a row of NA for station B, not just row 2
df[which(df$temp_c > 21), ]     # row 2 only: which() drops the NA
subset(df, temp_c > 21)         # row 2 only; dplyr::filter() does too
```


## Attached packages mask each other {#sec-attach}

`library(pkg)` attaches a package: its functions can then be called by their
plain names, and a function of a package attached later hides one of the same
name from an earlier package, as `dplyr::filter` hides `stats::filter`. R only
prints a message when it happens. `pkg::fun()` calls a function by its package
and is unambiguous. Use `library()` at the top of a script, and `::` in a
package, where the `NAMESPACE` file declares what is imported.


# Essential syntax {#sec-syntax}

The following is the part of R that most research code is made of.


## Values and collections {#sec-values}

```r
n <- 3L                       # an integer; 3 is a double
rate <- 0.05                  # a double; assign with <-
name <- "station-7"
ok <- TRUE                    # write TRUE and FALSE, never T and F

ages <- c(ana = 31, bo = 28)  # a named vector
ages["ana"]                   # 31
station <- list(name = "A", lat = 52.5, tags = c("coast", "tide"))
station$name                  # "A"
station[["lat"]]              # 52.5, one element; [ ] gives a sub-list

paste("Station", name, "has", length(values), "values")
sprintf("%s: %.2f", name, rate)   # "station-7: 0.05"
```

A data frame is a list of equally long columns:

```r
df$temp_k <- df$temp_c + 273.15     # a new column
df[df$station == "A", "temp_c"]     # rows by condition, one column
nrow(df); ncol(df); names(df); str(df)
```


## Conditionals and loops {#sec-control}

```r
if (rate > 0.1) {
  print("high")
} else if (rate > 0) {
  print("low")
} else {
  print("zero")
}

for (i in seq_along(values)) {        # with the index
  cat(i, values[i], "\n")
}
for (v in values) print(v)            # over the items
while (n > 0) n <- n - 1              # break and next work as usual

ifelse(values > 3, "warm", "cold")    # if, for a whole vector
vapply(values, function(v) v^2, numeric(1))      # apply, with the type
lapply(split(df$temp_c, df$station), mean, na.rm = TRUE)   # per group
```

The condition of an `if` must be a single `TRUE` or `FALSE`; a longer vector is
an error since R 4.2, and an `NA` is an error as well. Prefer `vapply()` to
`sapply()`: `sapply()` guesses the type of its result, and returns an empty
`list()` for empty input where `vapply()` returns an empty vector of the stated
type.


## Functions {#sec-functions}

```r
#' Mean drift rate of a station
#'
#' @param distance_m Distance moved, in meters.
#' @param days Time span, in days; must be positive.
#' @param per_year If `TRUE`, return meters per year instead of per day.
#' @return The rate, in meters per day or per year.
#' @export
drift_rate <- function(distance_m, days, per_year = FALSE) {
  if (days <= 0) {
    stop("`days` must be positive, got ", days, call. = FALSE)
  }
  rate <- distance_m / days
  if (per_year) rate * 365.25 else rate
}

drift_rate(12, 30)                          # by position
drift_rate(12, days = 30, per_year = TRUE)  # by name
```

The value of the last expression is the return value; `return()` is for an
early exit. Arguments are evaluated when first used, not when the function is
called. The tidyverse packages use this to let a call refer to a column by its
bare name, as in `filter(df, temp_c > 21)`, while the base functions need
`df$temp_c`.


## Errors {#sec-errors}

```r
result <- tryCatch(
  drift_rate(12, 0),
  error = function(e) {
    message("skipped: ", conditionMessage(e))
    NA_real_
  }
)
```

`stop()` raises an error for what the caller must fix, and `warning()` warns of
what the result can survive ([](../principles/design.qmd#sec-output)). Catch
only what you can handle.


## Files and paths {#sec-files}

```r
path <- file.path("data", "stations.csv")   # joins with the right separator
df <- read.csv(path)                        # or readr::read_csv()
write.csv(df, path, row.names = FALSE)
saveRDS(df, "df.rds")                       # any R object, exactly
df <- readRDS("df.rds")
list.files("data", pattern = "\\.csv$", full.names = TRUE)
```


## Tables and models {#sec-tables}

The tidyverse, above all dplyr, expresses table operations as a pipeline of
verbs, connected by the native pipe `|>` (R 4.1 and later):

```r
library(dplyr)

df |>
  filter(!is.na(temp_c), temp_c > 15) |>        # rows
  mutate(temp_k = temp_c + 273.15) |>           # new columns
  group_by(station) |>
  summarise(mean_c = mean(temp_c), n = n())     # one row per group

left_join(df, stations, by = "station")         # join two tables
```

A model is a function of a formula, with the response left of `~` and the
predictors right of it, and of the data:

```r
fit <- lm(temp_c ~ depth_m, data = measurements)
coef(fit)             # the estimates
summary(fit)          # estimates, standard errors, tests, R squared
predict(fit, newdata = data.frame(depth_m = 25))
```

Defaults are part of the API
([](../principles/design.qmd#sec-numeric-defaults)): `sd()` divides by `n - 1`,
the sample standard deviation, where `numpy.std()` divides by `n`.


# Tooling {#sec-tooling}

| Job | Tool |
|-------------------------------|---------------------------------------------|
| R version | rig, or the module or container image of the cluster |
| Packages, lock file | renv; Bioconductor packages through `BiocManager` |
| Package skeleton and development | usethis, devtools |
| Tests | testthat |
| Reference documentation | roxygen2, built into a website with pkgdown |
| Lint and format | lintr, styler |
| Reports | Quarto, R Markdown |


## The packages of a project with renv {#sec-renv-usage}

renv gives a project its own library of packages and records their exact
versions in `renv.lock`:

```r
renv::init()           # a project library and renv.lock, for this directory
renv::install("dplyr") # install a package into the project library
renv::snapshot()       # record the installed versions in renv.lock
renv::restore()        # install exactly what renv.lock says
renv::status()         # does the library match the lock file?
```

Commit `renv.lock`, and not the library `renv/library/`. renv records the
version of R as well but does not install it, so a rebuilt environment needs
the same R, for example from a container image
([](../tools/containers/index.qmd)).


## A package with devtools {#sec-package}

Code that is used more than once belongs in a package
([](../principles/design.qmd#sec-library)), not in a script that is `source()`d:

```r
usethis::create_package("stationfit")   # DESCRIPTION, NAMESPACE, R/
usethis::use_testthat()                 # tests/testthat/
usethis::use_r("drift")                 # a new file R/drift.R
devtools::load_all()                    # load the code without installing
devtools::document()                    # roxygen comments to man/ and NAMESPACE
devtools::test()                        # run the tests
devtools::check()                       # R CMD check: code, docs, and tests
```

`R CMD check`, which `devtools::check()` runs, tests that the package installs,
that its documentation is complete and matches the code, and that its examples
and tests pass. It is the standard that CRAN applies, so run it on every
change.


## Test with testthat {#sec-testthat}

Tests are files `tests/testthat/test-*.R` with calls of `test_that()`:

```r
test_that("drift_rate gives meters per day", {
  expect_equal(drift_rate(12, 30), 0.4)       # with a tolerance of 1.5e-8
  expect_error(drift_rate(12, 0), "positive") # and the message matches
})
```

`expect_equal()` compares with a tolerance and `expect_identical()` exactly
([](../principles/testing.qmd#sec-float-tests)); use the first for numbers
that were computed.


# Rules {#sec-rules}


## Use seq_len() and seq_along(), not 1:n {#sec-seq}

A loop over the indices of a vector should use `seq_along(x)`, and one over a
count `seq_len(n)`. `1:n` is not empty when `n` is zero but `c(1, 0)`, so the
loop body runs twice, with `i` equal to 1 and 0, on elements that do not exist,
and indexing an empty vector gives `NA` and nothing instead of an error
([](../principles/design.qmd#sec-loud)). An empty vector is a common case, for
example after a filter that kept no row, and `seq_len(0)` and `seq_along(x)`
are empty then, as the loop needs.


## Decide what happens to NA {#sec-na-rm}

Code must not drop missing values without saying so. `na.rm = TRUE` turns a
loud `NA` into a silent smaller sample, and the result looks as valid as
before. Set it only where dropping is the intended policy, make it a parameter
of your own function when the caller may want the other choice, and state the
policy in the documentation and the count of dropped values in the output
([](../principles/design.qmd#sec-missing)). Where an `NA` is a defect, check
for it with `anyNA()` and stop.


## Lock the packages with renv {#sec-renv}

An analysis or a workflow should run with a project library whose versions are
locked by renv, and commit `renv.lock` with the code
([](../principles/design.qmd#sec-pin)). A package declares in `DESCRIPTION`
the packages it imports, with the lowest version that works, and leaves the
exact versions to the project that uses it. As renv does not lock R itself,
record the version of R with the results as well, or run in a container image
([](../principles/design.qmd#sec-traceability)).


## Document every exported function with roxygen {#sec-roxygen}

An exported function should have roxygen comments, written next to the
function, that state what it computes and, for every parameter and the return
value, its meaning, shape, unit, and default
([](../principles/documenting.qmd#sec-reference)). `devtools::document()`
turns them into the help pages, which `R CMD check` compares with the code, so
a parameter that is documented but missing, or the other way round, is
reported, and pkgdown builds the website from them. Mark with `@export` only
what users are meant to call; everything else is internal and free to change
([](../principles/design.qmd#sec-stable-api)).
